scenes.narration: Two exams sit at the center of this course: the Solutions Architect Associate — officially S A A, C zero three — and the Solutions Architect Professional, S A P, C zero two. From here on we'll just call them the associate exam and the professional exam. The associate exam gives you sixty five questions in a hundred and thirty minutes, and a pass mark of seven hundred twenty out of a thousand. The professional exam is longer and harder: seventy five questions, a hundred and eighty minutes, and a pass mark of seven hundred fifty. Both are scored against four weighted domains, and that weighting is the single most important fact in this chapter.

The most common mistake here isn't laziness, it's the opposite. Trying to learn every AWS service to the same depth. Logging hours of video content without ever touching the console. Tracking progress by hours studied instead of by which domains you're actually weak in. All three feel like diligence. All three are the wrong instinct, and the exam's own scoring math is about to tell us why.

props.heading: “I'll just learn all of AWS”
bullets: The completionist: study 200-plus AWS services to equal depth before sitting the exam.
The passive binge-watcher: hours of video content, almost no hands-on practice.
The hours-logged tracker: measuring progress by study time, not by weak-domain coverage.

scenes.narration: Lay the two exams side by side and the differences are concrete, not vibes. Associate: sixty five questions, a hundred thirty minutes, pass at seven twenty. Professional: seventy five questions, a hundred eighty minutes, pass at seven fifty, and roughly double the fee. Each exam is also weighted differently. Associate leans hardest on secure architectures at thirty percent. Professional leans hardest on designing for new solutions at twenty nine percent.

props.heading: Side by side, not just longer or shorter

scenes.narration: Here's why the weighting matters more than raw coverage. On the associate exam, security architecture alone is thirty percent of your score. On the professional exam, designing for new solutions edges out organizational complexity, twenty nine to twenty six. Study time that ignores this shape is study time spent inefficiently, no matter how many hours you log.

The correct approach follows directly from the blueprint. Allocate your hours proportional to each domain's weight. Build hands-on fundamentals instead of just watching videos. Learn the decision frameworks: when do you actually reach for one service over another. Take timed practice exams under real conditions. Drill whichever domain your practice scores expose as weakest. And only schedule the real exam once your practice scores are consistently at your target, not on a fixed calendar date.

props.heading: Derived from the blueprint, not from habit
steps: Allocate hours by domain weight, not evenly
Build AWS fundamentals hands-on, not just watched
Learn the decision frameworks — when to choose what
Take timed practice exams under real conditions
Drill whichever domain is weakest in practice
Gate exam-day scheduling on consistent scores

scenes.narration: This is the single most useful artifact in the chapter — a framework that maps your starting point to a path. No cloud background: budget around a hundred twenty to a hundred fifty hours before the associate exam, weighted toward fundamentals and hands-on labs. Some general I T experience without AWS: expect eighty to a hundred hours. Already working with AWS day to day: you can often move to the professional exam after a lighter associate pass, fifty to seventy hours each, focused on decision frameworks. And if you're already operating at architect level, you can attempt the professional exam directly, spending most of your time on scenario practice and drilling whatever your practice scores expose as weak.

props.kicker: THE ONE FRAMEWORK THAT MATTERS MOST
props.heading: Which exam first, and for how many hours

scenes.narration: Two files anchor every AWS CLI setup. A config file holding your default region and output format per named profile. A credentials file holding the actual keys — never the same file, and never committed to git. A cache directory underneath holds short-lived session tokens you'll rarely touch directly.

props.kicker: THE CLI, BEFORE YOU NEED IT
props.heading: Your ~/.aws/ directory
lines: ├── config          # region, output format, per named profile
├── credentials      # access key + secret key — never commit this

scenes.narration: You don't need to be a CLI expert for either exam, but a few commands should feel familiar. `aws configure` sets your access key, secret key, default region, and output format. `aws sts get-caller-identity` is the fastest way to confirm exactly which account and identity your credentials resolve to — invaluable once you're juggling multiple profiles. And targeting a named profile lets you point any command at a specific set of credentials instead of your default. Exam questions about IAM policies and cross-account access read very differently once you've actually run these commands yourself.

Take a concrete case. Diego has three years of backend engineering experience but has never worked with AWS professionally, and his team is migrating in four months while he studies ten hours a week. Run him through the framework: his gap isn't architectural judgment, it's AWS-specific knowledge. So he starts with the associate exam, and he weights his hours toward hands-on fundamentals rather than decision-framework drilling he doesn't yet have the vocabulary to use.

scenes.narration: Try these before we reveal the answers. First: a candidate skips two of the four domains entirely and plans to guess — is that fatal on its own? Second, and this one trips up even experienced engineers: on a multiple-response question, is partial credit given for getting some, but not all, of the correct options?

questions.prompt: A candidate skips studying two of the four exam domains entirely, planning to guess on those questions. Which is true?
options: They automatically fail, regardless of score on the other domains.
There's no per-domain minimum — a strong overall score can still pass despite two weak domains.
Skipped domains are simply not scored.
The exam blocks submission until every domain has a confident answer.

questions.prompt: On a multiple-response question, no partial credit is given for selecting 2 of 3 correct options. What does this mean for elimination strategy?
options: Guessing broadly increases expected score, so select every plausible option.
You need every correct option and zero incorrect ones — eliminate confidently wrong options first.
Multiple-response questions are simply weighted less than single-answer ones.
Selecting one extra correct-looking option never hurts your score.

scenes.narration: Here's why. There's no domain gate on either exam — it's one composite weighted score, so skipping domains is risky, but not automatically disqualifying. And multiple-response questions give zero partial credit: two correct picks out of three needed scores identically to zero correct. That's exactly why elimination strategy matters more than raw recall — one wrong extra selection can turn a mostly-right answer into a complete miss.

answers.prompt: A candidate skips two of four domains entirely, planning to guess.
answers.correct: No per-domain minimum — a strong overall score can still pass.
answers.rationale: There's no domain gate on either exam — your score is a single weighted composite. It's a bad strategy because you're leaving 30%-plus of the exam to chance, but it isn't automatically disqualifying the way people assume.

answers.correct: You need every correct option and zero incorrect ones.
answers.rationale: There's no partial credit: selecting two of three correct options scores exactly the same as selecting zero. A single plausible-but-wrong extra pick can turn a mostly-correct selection into a full miss — eliminate confidently wrong answers before committing.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. The two exams are weighted differently, not just longer or shorter. There's no domain-gate minimum, but there's also no partial credit on multiple-response questions — both cut against sloppy guessing. Study hours should track the blueprint's weights, not habit. The framework you just saw should be the first thing you consult, before you open a single service's documentation. And elimination strategy will get you further than raw memorization. Next: IAM, the service almost every other domain quietly depends on.

The starting-point framework maps your experience to a path and an hour budget — consult it first.
